Root cause (test-authoring bug, NOT a production defect): the test's mock 'globalThis.fetch' returns '{ id, description: ..., updatedAt: ... }' (field named 'description'), but the CLIENT code under test (packages/apra-fleet-se/auto-sprint/viewer-extensions.mjs loadBeadDescription(), line ~541) reads 'data.text', and the REAL server-side wire contract (packages/apra-fleet-workflow/src/viewer/index.mjs's GET /extensions/:extId/detail/:itemId route, ~line 1069) responds with '{ id, text, updatedAt }' -- 'text', never 'description'. The client's detailLookup hook contract (beadsExtension.detailLookup, viewer-extensions.mjs ~line 436) is explicitly documented to return '{text, updatedAt}' specifically so core/client code never has to know bd's raw field name ('description'). The test's mock fetch simply used the wrong field name for the wire shape it is simulating; production code and the real wire contract already agree with each other and are NOT the source of the mismatch.
Test: node scripts/run-integ-suites.mjs full 85-file real-bd pass; viewer-perf-regression-e2e.test.mjs in integ-suite-status.json, failures[] for the 3 tests named above.

Fix direction: update the test's mock fetch responses in this describe block from '{ id, description, updatedAt }' to '{ id, text, updatedAt }' to match the real wire contract. This is test code -- integ-test-runner does not modify test code, filing for a doer/developer to fix.

title: [integ] golden-transcript real-bd divergence: D-pull gating skips 'bd dolt pull' in no-remote scratch dir, stale golden
description: Under real bd (APRA_FLEET_BD_MOCK=off), golden-transcript.test.mjs test 'mock sprint happy-path dispatch sequence matches the committed snapshot' FAILS at JSONL line 5 (dispatch seq 4): GOLDEN expects 'bd dolt pull', ACTUAL is 'bd list --all --limit 0 --json'. The committed golden (fixtures/golden-transcript/mock-sprint-happy-path.jsonl, last regenerated in adec2dce/eft.35) still contains the D-pull, but the D-pull gating that landed in adec2dce ('gate D-pull the same way D-push is gated') now SKIPS 'bd dolt pull' when the scratch bd-init dir has no configured sync.remote. So the real-mode dispatch sequence no longer contains the D-pull the golden expects. The test PASSES in mock mode (APRA_FLEET_BD_MOCK=1, 2/2) because mock mode synthesizes the dolt-sync brackets as present no-ops, so the golden now only matches mock-mode dispatch, making the test mode-dependent. title: [viewer] Show elapsed-since-start on running activities (right edge), not just final duration
description:
USER ENHANCEMENT (2026-07-21). Today a running AGENT dispatch shows nothing
on its right edge until it finishes, when the full duration appears. During
a long prompt (5-15 min) the user cannot tell running from stuck.

FIX: for activities with isRunning true and no final duration, render
elapsed time since start at the row's right edge (where the final duration
will eventually appear): now - startTime, formatted like the final duration
(0s, 5s, 10s, 1m 20s...). Both fields already exist in the state payload
(sample real activity keys include startTime and isRunning) -- this is a
CLIENT-side render change only, no wire-format change.

EXPLICITLY NOT REQUIRED: an automatic per-second ticking timer. The value
just needs to be correct whenever the page renders -- which the existing
poll/refresh cycle already provides (each poll repaint recomputes it), and
a manual refresh must show the right elapsed value. If a trivial
setInterval repaint of ONLY these labels is added later it must not
regress snappiness (standing eft.27 constraint) -- but it is out of scope
for acceptance.

ACCEPTANCE:
1. A running agent/command activity row shows a nonzero, monotonically
   increasing elapsed value across successive polls/refreshes.
2. On completion the label is replaced by the final duration exactly as
   today.
3. No new timers required for acceptance; no measurable render-time
   regression on a 500+ activity tree.

FINDING: no repo SOURCE/test file contains a hardcoded broad taskkill/pkill/Stop-Process (confirmed via repo-wide grep, apra-fleet-client's two hits are targeted: a liveness-check `process.kill(pid, 0)` and a specific child-handle `.kill()`). But AGENT-EXECUTED Bash commands (not baked into the repo, run ad-hoc by doers mid-turn) do this routinely:
  - A subagent on 2026-07-12 ran a genuinely broad `taskkill //F //IM node.exe` (kills EVERY node.exe on the machine by image name) -- 6 days before either crash, so not a direct hit, but proves this exact dangerous pattern has been used in this environment before.
  - Doer session a5099188-08bf-40ed-9e19-2a4f55fb39a3 ([yysru], working eft.2.2/eft.2.3 during run2) ran `taskkill //F //PID 50600 //T; taskkill //F //PID 26192 //T` at 2026-07-18T06:53:11Z (~02:53:11 local) -- PID-targeted (not broad-by-name), but `//T` kills the entire process tree rooted at each PID, and this ran only ~10 minutes before run2's orchestrator log went silent (03:03:08 local). The doer's own narration shows it was cleaning up a background test-server process it had itself started (eft.2.2/2.3 test run), matching the exact 'stale port-holding node.exe, manually taskkill'd' pattern already documented in apra-fleet-eft.13.

NOT PROVEN: I did not capture the orchestrator's own node.exe PID at launch time for either run1 (b0wm0tejb) or run2 (baspge4p1), so I cannot directly confirm either taskkill's target PID(s) matched the orchestrator's actual PID. Windows PID reuse (a PID captured via tasklist/netstat by the doer, then killed after the OS had already recycled that same PID number for an unrelated process -- e.g. the orchestrator, launched around the same time) is a plausible race that would explain an accidental hit without any broad by-name kill being involved at all.

RECOMMENDATION FOR NEXT RUN (not yet done, needs a decision on whether/when to relaunch):
  1. Immediately after launching, capture and log the orchestrator's own node.exe PID (e.g. `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "name='node.exe'" | ? CommandLine -match 'cli.mjs'`).
  2. Poll `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "name='node.exe'"` (PID, CreationDate, CommandLine, ParentProcessId) every 2-3 minutes for the whole run, so any future death can be cross-referenced PID-for-PID against every taskkill any doer ran in that window (grep each active session transcript for `taskkill`/`Stop-Process` the same way this investigation did, but now with a ground-truth orchestrator PID to compare against instead of only timestamp proximity).
  3. Separately, regardless of whether this specific mechanism is confirmed: recommend the fix direction already on file in apra-fleet-eft.13 (ephemeral test ports, best-effort scoped process-tree teardown) plus a stronger doer-level guardrail against `taskkill //IM node.exe` / any unscoped-by-name process kill, given it has already been used at least once in this environment's history.

title: fleet-sprint: TWO consecutive sprint runs died silently (~25-47 min in) while a doer sub-session was still actively working -- points to external kill of orchestrator process, not an app bug
description:
OBSERVED: Both auto-sprint runs for apra-fleet-eft died with the identical signature:
  - run1 (task b0wm0tejb): launched 2026-07-17 23:26:53, orchestrator log's last write 23:40:08 (~13 min). BUT the actively-dispatched doer sub-session (c61ec80b, streak [eytc7]) kept working and hit max_turns_reached (51 turns) at 23:44:01 -- 4 min AFTER the orchestrator log went silent. A retry sub-session (31e46e4f) continued working until at least 23:50:24. Real death (dashboard down, no node.exe alive) confirmed by ~00:02.
  - run2 (task baspge4p1): launched 2026-07-18 02:19:50, orchestrator log's last write 03:03:08 (~43 min), right after dispatching Streak [apra-fleet-eft.5, apra-fleet-eft.5.1]. BUT the actively-dispatched doer sub-session (d05aa1aa, streak [ks34t], doing real eft.5 ledger work -- git status showing src/supervisor/ledger.mjs, test/supervisor-ledger.test.mjs as legitimate in-progress output) kept working until at least 07:07:18 UTC (~03:07:18 local) -- 4 min after ITS orchestrator log also went silent. This task-notification arrived with status "killed".

PATTERN: in both runs, the same ~4-minute gap between (a) the orchestrator's own log going silent and (b) the actively-dispatched CHILD doer session's last recorded activity. Neither run shows a crash signature (no stack trace, no uncaught exception, no "Error:" line, no Windows APPCRASH event for node.exe in either window -- checked via Get-WinEvent). The doer sessions were not stuck/looping either: run1's hit a legitimate max_turns cap doing real multi-file refactor work; run2's was mid-`git status` on real, coherent feature work.

ANALYSIS:
1. This is NOT the same root cause as apra-fleet-eft.13 (EADDRINUSE/orphaned-port cascade) -- neither log shows a port conflict or Transport-closed cascade as the terminal event. run2 DID show 3x "Authentication failed on fleet-reorg" + one 930s dispatch timeout mid-run (matches this operator's known local-member-OAuth-expiry failure mode), but the sprint visibly recovered from that and successfully completed 3 more streaks (eft.3, eft.4) afterward -- so auth expiry is a real, separate, already-known issue but not what killed either run.
2. Both orchestrator processes were launched via Bash `run_in_background` (harness-tracked backgrounding, chosen specifically as the non-evasive alternative to the README's raw `&`+`disown` recipe -- see auto-sprint-1). The consistent "child briefly outlives orchestrator by ~4 min, both eventually killed with no crash signature" pattern across two independent runs, at two very different elapsed-time points (13 min vs 43 min -- ruling out a fixed short timeout), is more consistent with an EXTERNAL termination of the orchestrator's process (and, shortly after, its live children) than with any bug inside runner.js or cli.mjs.
3. HYPOTHESIS (not yet confirmed): the harness's `run_in_background` may scope the spawned node.exe process to a Windows Job Object tied to the underlying shell/pty session, and something in that shell's lifecycle (recycling, an idle/keepalive boundary, or cleanup tied to this orchestrating conversation's own tool-call cadence) may be tearing down that Job Object periodically -- which would kill the orchestrator immediately but leave its already-spawned grandchild CLI doer sessions (spawned as more independent processes, possibly outside the same Job Object) to finish their current turn before also disappearing. This would mean harness-tracked backgrounding does NOT reliably protect a 30-60+ minute sprint from the exact "tool-call process group killed" failure mode the suspect README warned about (auto-sprint-1) -- ironically for a different reason than the README's own (false) justification.
4. NOT YET RULED OUT: OS-level resource pressure (memory climbed from ~11.2GB/16GB at run1 to ~11.9GB/16GB at run2 check, both around 70% system memory) silently killing the process without a WER crash report is possible but less likely to produce the exact same ~4-minute child-outlives-parent gap twice.

RECOMMENDATION: if a third run is attempted, capture `wmic process where name='node.exe' get ProcessId,CreationDate,ParentProcessId` (or Get-CimInstance Win32_Process) polled every few minutes throughout the run, so a future death can be correlated against exact PID/parent-PID lifecycle instead of reconstructed after the fact from session-transcript timestamps. Also worth asking the harness/environment owner directly whether background Bash tasks in this session type have an enforced maximum lifetime.
notes: triage 2026-08-09 (autosprint-internals batch): STALE-LOW-VALUE, environment has changed out from under it. NAMING -- the whole auto-sprint-N bead namespace predates the 2026-07-26 rename (commit 058160e7) and means fleet-sprint, NOT the /auto-sprint skill: this bead's references are cli.mjs, runner.js, the dashboard and 'apra-fleet workflow auto-sprint' launches. Corroborated by sibling auto-sprint-1's own close note, which says 'fleet-sprint/docs/README.md (post-rename)'. Title corrected. WHY STALE: (a) the core hypothesis was that the HARNESS's Bash run_in_background Job Object was tearing down the orchestrator -- sprints are no longer launched that way; they are spawned by the supervisor (src/supervisor/spawner.mjs, which records the child pid at :312/:381) and, per current operating convention, as detached SEA-binary runs. (b) The bead's own top recommendation (capture the orchestrator PID at launch and poll process liveness so a future death can be correlated PID-for-PID) is now IMPLEMENTED: src/supervisor/watchdog.mjs classifies a vanished sprint as 'no longer alive ... classified CRASHED by the PID-liveness watchdog' (:459) and reconcile.mjs:174 handles the no-recorded-pid case. (c) No recurrence in ~3 weeks of sprints since 2026-07-18. Not closed -- the two deaths were never root-caused -- but P0 is no longer defensible; lowered P0 -> P3 as an unreproduced historical investigation.

title: fleet-sprint: add an explicit pause/resume control distinct from hard Stop
description:
Idea surfaced while running the apra-fleet-7pm auto-sprint live: the
dashboard currently only exposes a hard 'Stop' (POST /stop, forcibly cancels
the workflow via `FleetWorkflow.requestStop()` -> aborts every in-flight
`agent()`/`command()` via `AbortController`, see
packages/apra-fleet-workflow/src/viewer/index.mjs:521 and
src/workflow/index.mjs:460). We verified the system is ALREADY resumable in
practice at the granularity of a full process restart -- beads (task state)
and git (commits) are the durable source of truth, so relaunching the
identical CLI invocation after a stop/crash correctly skips already-closed
tasks and picks up remaining open work.

What's missing is a deliberate, first-class pause/resume mechanism that is
cheaper and more graceful than "kill the process and relaunch," and that
resumes the SAME run rather than re-deriving everything from beads state and
re-running Plan from scratch.

## Key finding: the substrate for this already exists

`packages/apra-fleet-workflow`'s engine already has a journal/replay system
(`journal.mjs`, `computeActivityKey`, `journalEnabled`, `completedByKey`,
`diverged`) that backs instant-replay resume for `agent()`/`command()` calls
-- this is the same mechanism the Workflow tool's `resumeFromRunId` exposes:
re-running a script replays every already-completed activity from the
journal cache instantly, and only the first new/changed call executes live.
Pause/resume does not need a new persistence layer -- it needs a new
SUSPEND primitive built on the journal, distinct from both normal
completion and `requestStop()`'s hard cancellation.

## Proposed design: `interrupt()` as a journaled activity type

Modeled on LangGraph's `interrupt()` (raises inside a running graph node,
checkpoints state, halts until a human supplies a resume value, then
continues that exact node with the value in hand):

1. **New script-level primitive**: `await interrupt(checkpointName, {
   message, schema? })`, callable from `runner.js` at safe boundaries only
   (between cycles, after Deploy before Integ-Test, before Publish PR --
   never mid-agent-dispatch). Safe boundaries matter: unlike a hard Stop,
   Pause must never leave an `agent()` call half-abandoned, so it can only
   suspend at points the script itself designates, not at arbitrary
   moments an external Pause button is pressed.

2. **On first execution** (not yet in the journal): `interrupt()` writes a
   new journal entry of type `interrupt` (sequence-numbered like `agent`/
   `command` entries), containing `checkpointName`, `message`, and current
   script-level state useful for the dashboard to render (phase, cycle,
   round, streak -- the same state bead 9ub already names). It then emits
   an `interrupt` event (mirrors the existing `state`/`log`/`end` events in
   viewer/index.mjs) and the run's `executeFile()` promise resolves with
   status `'paused'` -- a new terminal status distinct from `'completed'`,
   `'cancelled'`, `'failed'`. Critically this is NOT `requestStop()`: no
   `AbortController` fires, nothing in flight is rejected, because by
   construction nothing is in flight at a designated checkpoint.

3. **Dashboard**: a `Pause` control becomes meaningful as "pause at the
   next checkpoint" (sets a flag the next `interrupt()` call checks) rather
   than "pause now" -- this is the honest UX given #1's constraint, and
   should be presented as such (e.g. "Pausing after current phase..." while
   waiting, not an instant pause). Once paused, the dashboard renders the
   `interrupt` event's `message`/checkpoint like a card, with a `Resume`
   button (and, if `schema` was supplied, an input form -- mirrors
   LangGraph's `Command(resume=value)` payload; e.g. a checkpoint before
   Publish PR could ask "proceed with PR title: <draft>?" and accept an
   edited title as the resume value).

4. **Resume**: `POST /resume { runId, value }` re-invokes
   `WorkflowEngine.executeFile()` with `journalEnabled: true` and the
   persisted journal for `runId`. Every activity before the `interrupt()`
   call (all completed `agent()`/`command()` calls, and the `interrupt`
   entry itself) replays from cache -- cheap, no re-dispatch, no re-running
   Plan. When the script reaches the SAME `interrupt()` call again, instead
   of suspending a second time, it returns the supplied `value` (or
   `undefined` if none was needed) and the script continues live from
   there. This is the exact mechanism that already makes `resumeFromRunId`
   work for `agent()` -- `interrupt()` is "the same replay machinery,
   generalized to a script-level suspend point instead of just an agent
   dispatch."

5. **`bin/cli.mjs` surface**: a `--resume-run-id <id>` flag, so the CLI
   launch this feeds from the dashboard doesn't need to reconstruct any
   auto-sprint-specific state -- it just hands the runId to
   `executeFile()` and the journal does the rest.

## Open questions / scoping notes (why this stays a backlog idea, not
scheduled work)

- Where exactly in `runner.js` do `interrupt()` checkpoints make sense?
  Candidates: end of each outer cycle, after Deploy succeeds and before
  Integ-Test runs (a natural "confirm before touching anything
  test-adjacent" point), before Publish PR (confirm PR title/description).
  Needs a pass through the phase list to pick boundaries that are both
  safe (no abandoned in-flight work) and useful (a human would actually
  want to intervene there).
- Interaction with the existing phase-resume/concurrency-lock work already
  landed in apra-pm (PR #19) -- needs a check that a second `executeFile()`
  invocation for the same `runId` doesn't race the lock that work put in
  place.
- Journal storage lifetime/location for a PAUSED (not finished) run --
  existing journal files are presumably write-once-per-run; pausing needs
  the journal kept live/appendable across the gap between suspend and
  resume, including across a full process restart if the dashboard's Node
  process itself needs to come down while paused.
- Whether `interrupt()` should be a generic `packages/apra-fleet-workflow`
  engine primitive (usable by any workflow script) or something auto-sprint
  specific in `runner.js` -- leaning toward the former since the journal
  machinery it rides on lives in the engine, not in auto-sprint.

Do not start without further design discussion -- this description is a
starting proposal, not an approved spec.
notes: triage 2026-08-09 (autosprint-internals batch): NEEDS-DEEPER-DESIGN, unchanged, still valid. NAMING -- 'Auto-sprint' is STALE for fleet-sprint: every code reference in the body is packages/apra-fleet-workflow/src/viewer/index.mjs, src/workflow/index.mjs and fleet-sprint/runner.js (the /auto-sprint skill has no dashboard and no Stop endpoint at all). Title corrected. Verified NOT implemented: grep across packages/apra-fleet-workflow/src/ finds no interrupt() primitive, no 'paused' terminal status, no /resume route and no --resume-run-id flag; the journal substrate the proposal rides on does still exist (workflow/journal.mjs, journalEnabled/replay at workflow/index.mjs:678,1633), so the design's central premise holds. Partially overtaken by a coarser mechanism worth folding into any redesign: the supervisor now ships Stop AND Restart controls (src/supervisor/dashboard.mjs:269,349) plus readopt.mjs/reconcile.mjs/watchdog.mjs, i.e. process-restart-granularity resume is now first-class -- which is exactly the 'kill and relaunch' baseline this bead wanted something cheaper than. Keep at P3, keep the do-not-start-without-design-discussion caveat.

title: [bug] pm-skill planner.md/plan-reviewer.md use literal Claude model names in task metadata, inconsistent with apra-fleet-se's cheap/standard/premium tier vocabulary
description:
Discovered live during apra-fleet-7pm's real auto-sprint run (2026-07-13). The standalone `planner` and `plan-reviewer` subagents (installed from packages/apra-fleet-se/apra-pm's agents/planner.md, agents/plan-reviewer.md -- generic pm-skill agents, not apra-fleet-se-specific) write/expect task metadata like `{"model": "opus"}` / `{"model": "sonnet"}` -- literal Claude model family names.

But packages/apra-fleet-se/auto-sprint/runner.js's real dispatch (FIXED_ROLE_TIER, apra-fleet-dv5) expects the three literal tier strings 'cheap'/'standard'/'premium' instead -- de-hardcoding literal model names was the entire point of apra-fleet-dv5.

When I used the generic `planner` agent to build apra-fleet-7pm's DAG (ahead of running auto-sprint against it) and had `plan-reviewer` review it, both used the opus/sonnet vocabulary, matching planner.md's own documented convention. auto-sprint's OWN internal Plan phase (running as part of the real sprint, not the standalone agent) caught the mismatch and silently rewrote all 14 tasks' metadata to the tier vocabulary before proceeding -- so this round self-healed, but it cost an extra rewrite pass and could easily NOT self-heal for a differently-worded task set (there's no guarantee auto-sprint's internal planner always catches every task, e.g. if it deems some already fine and doesn't compare against the full ready-list from a fresh angle).

Root cause: packages/apra-fleet-se/apra-pm's planner.md/plan-reviewer.md were written independently of, and predate, apra-fleet-dv5's tier-vocabulary contract, and were never updated to match it.
acceptance_criteria: Decide and document the correct relationship: either (a) update vendor/apra-pm's planner.md/plan-reviewer.md to use the cheap/standard/premium tier vocabulary when the target is an apra-fleet-se auto-sprint run (possibly conditioned on some signal distinguishing 'pm skill standalone sprint' from 'apra-fleet-se auto-sprint target'), or (b) make auto-sprint's runner.js Plan phase's self-correction an explicit, tested, always-on step (not incidental) with a warning surfaced when a rewrite happens, so users know their upstream planning tool used the wrong vocabulary. Either way, the two docs should stop silently disagreeing.
notes: ALREADY-FIXED-OR-DUPLICATE. Verified directly: packages/apra-fleet-se/apra-pm/agents/planner.md (lines 107-150) and agents/plan-reviewer.md (lines 120-170) already document and enforce the cheap/standard/premium tier vocabulary described in apra-fleet-dv5 (e.g. planner.md:107 'bd create ... --metadata {"model": "<cheap|standard|premium>"}', plan-reviewer.md:169-170 sample output using 'standard'/'cheap'). The literal Claude model-name convention (opus/sonnet) this bug describes as planner.md's 'own documented convention' is no longer present in either file. The self-heal-cost concern in the bug (auto-sprint's Plan phase silently rewriting mismatched metadata) may still be worth hardening per the bead's acceptance criteria option (b), but the root-cause premise -- that vendor/apra-pm's planner/plan-reviewer docs disagree with the tier vocabulary -- no longer holds. Closing as fixed/no-longer-reproducible; reopen with a fresh repro if the docs regress.
close_reason: planner.md/plan-reviewer.md already use cheap/standard/premium tier vocabulary throughout (verified by direct read); the described inconsistency no longer exists.

title: Beads workflow should handle/self-fix overly-permissive .beads dir permissions gracefully
description:
Observed on fleet-lin-dev1 (new member, freshly registered/cloned repo at /home/akhil/git/apra-fleet-dev1):

  Warning: /home/akhil/git/apra-fleet-dev1/.beads has permissions 0775 (recommended: 0700).
  Run: chmod 700 /home/akhil/git/apra-fleet-dev1/.beads

This is a bd/beads-side warning surfaced during normal workflow use on a fresh clone -- the .beads directory ends up group/world-readable+executable (0775) instead of the recommended owner-only 0700, likely inherited from the parent directory's umask at clone/init time rather than anything bd itself sets deliberately.

Currently this just prints a warning and leaves it to the operator to notice and manually chmod it. For a fleet member (headless, unattended dispatch), nobody is watching stdout for this warning -- it should be handled gracefully by our workflow instead of relying on a human to spot and fix it:
- Detect the overly-permissive .beads dir before/during workflow bootstrap (fleet-sprint / fleet-se sandbox setup, member registration, or wherever we first touch a fresh clone's .beads dir) and auto-correct it (chmod 700) rather than just warning.
- Or, if auto-correcting is undesirable for some reason (e.g. a legitimate multi-user setup), at least surface the warning loudly enough that it reaches the dispatch logs / dashboard rather than being silently swallowed in a member's stdout.

Repro: register a new fleet member with a fresh git clone containing a .beads dir, run any bd command against it -- the permissions warning appears on stderr/stdout of that bd invocation.
notes: NEEDS-RESEARCH-ONLY. Grepped src/, packages/, and workflow bootstrap code for any existing .beads permission handling (0700/0775/chmod) -- found none; the bug is real and unaddressed. However, fixing it requires first identifying the correct hook point the bead itself leaves open as an either/or: where a fresh member clone's .beads dir is first touched (fleet-sprint/fleet-se sandbox setup vs member registration vs first bd invocation), and which remediation (auto-chmod vs loud-surfacing to dispatch logs/dashboard) is preferred for a headless fleet member. No existing scaffolding to hang a fix on was found in this pass, so this needs a short research/design spike (locate the bootstrap entry point) before it becomes pure implementation. Priority P4, non-blocking, no mutation beyond this note.

title: Document that 'apra-fleet install' must follow 'npm run build:binary' before standalone binary use
description:
Root cause (investigated 2026-07-26): the workflow-runtime version-skew warning ([warn] workflows in ~/.apra-fleet/workflows were installed by apra-fleet vX, but this binary is vY) is expected behavior per docs/workflow-subsystem-plan.md requirement R10, not a bug. Both versions are git-short-sha stamps: the binary's own version is baked in at 'npm run build:binary' time (scripts/build-sea.mjs), while the installed workflow runtime's version is stamped by 'apra-fleet install' (src/cli/install.ts). build:binary never calls install or refreshes ~/.apra-fleet/workflows, so rebuilding the binary without re-running install always produces this (harmless, non-fatal) warning on next launch. No code fix needed -- this is a docs/DX gap: nothing currently reminds the operator that 'apra-fleet install' must be re-run after every 'npm run build:binary' before launching the binary standalone (relevant to the delivered-binary-launch-convention pattern of building the SEA binary and launching it detached from ~/bin).

Suggested fix: add a line to the fleet-sprint-cli skill and/or README build docs noting the install-after-build requirement, so operators don't need to re-diagnose this each time they see the warning.

title: [follow-up] Drift detection: echo resolved model/tier on execute_prompt, verify against get_member_model_pricing (P4, not a prerequisite for dv5.5/.6)
description:
REVISED 2026-07-12: SUPERSEDED as the primary cost-accuracy mechanism. Per project-owner correction 3 on epic apra-fleet-dv5, real per-member cost tracking is now solved WITHOUT needing per-dispatch echo-back: tier->model resolution is deterministic and config-driven (src/tools/execute-prompt.ts resolveModelForTier(), each provider's modelTiers()/modelForTier()), so a new `get_member_model_pricing` MCP tool (apra-fleet-dv5.5) can answer "what does member X's premium tier cost" ahead of time, once per member per run, with no echo-back required. apra-fleet-dv5.6 wires that into apra-fleet-workflow's budget tracking as the primary pricing source, falling back to pricing.mjs's tier-band estimate only when unavailable.

This issue is NOT closed as invalid -- it retains narrower residual value: DRIFT DETECTION. A member's actual runtime resolution could theoretically diverge from its registered model_tiers config (e.g. a provider-side override, a manually-edited settings file the fleet server doesn't know about, a mid-run config change) in ways get_member_model_pricing's static/cached lookup would not catch. Echo-back would let the client verify "the model I was actually billed against matches the model I priced against" rather than trusting the static resolution stays true for the whole run. This is a correctness/verification enhancement on TOP of dv5.5/dv5.6's primary mechanism, not a prerequisite for it.

Scope (files, if/when taken up): src/tools/execute-prompt.ts (already computes resolvedModel/resolvedTier ~293-329 -- include both in the tool's result payload), packages/apra-fleet-client (surface them on the execute_prompt response), packages/apra-fleet-workflow/src/workflow/index.mjs (compare echoed resolvedModel against the pre-dispatch get_member_model_pricing-based price; log/flag a mismatch rather than silently trusting either source).

Priority lowered to P4: no longer blocking real per-member costing (that's apra-fleet-dv5.5/.6); this is now a drift-detection nice-to-have. Depends conceptually on apra-fleet-dv5.5/.6 landing first (there is no static price to compare an echo against otherwise).

Risks/unknowns: journal/replay compatibility for new activity fields; remote/relayed members (hub-spoke RelayStrategy) may not have the resolved model available at the same point; mixed fleets where some members echo and some do not must not double-count or fabricate.

Acceptance criteria (for the eventual implementer): a dispatch against a member with model_tiers configured shows the concrete resolved model in the workflow journal; if it disagrees with the price pre-computed via get_member_model_pricing, a warning is logged naming the discrepancy; absent an echo, behavior is unaffected (dv5.5/.6's static resolution is used as-is, unchanged).
notes: READY-AS-IS. title: [DEFERRED] Relay/NAT-traversal command execution -- revisit once fleet-dashboard's bidirectional WebSocket relay ships
description:
Explicitly deferred, not abandoned: fleet-dashboard's docs/architecture.md documents its own bidirectional WebSocket relay (member <-> cloud <-> browser/dashboard-initiated command push) as 'DESIGNED, NOT YET BUILT.' apra-fleet-reorg's own envelope/SSE/Postgres relay system (built during the hub-spoke migration sprint, src/services/relay-executor.ts, relay-request.ts, hub-client.ts, spoke.ts) proved the wire-protocol semantics (at-least-once delivery, TTL, redelivery, workspace isolation) but per this epic's scoping decision is not the production transport -- SSH remains the primary/permanent execution transport, and NAT-traversal relay is a secondary transport for machines SSH cannot reach, not a priority for the current bootstrap/sync-focused phase.

Revisit once: (a) fleet-dashboard ships its bidirectional WebSocket half, and (b) there is a concrete customer need for command execution against a machine SSH cannot reach. At that point, decide whether apra-fleet.exe's relay client speaks fleet-dashboard's WebSocket protocol (likely) or something else, using apra-fleet-reorg's already-built envelope semantics as the reference design.
acceptance_criteria: No action expected until explicitly reprioritized. This issue exists so the deferred decision and its rationale are not lost.
